Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette:
At nineteen, Emily had been married less than a year when she was assaulted, and she still describes her life as divided into before and after. The assault happened at night as she was walking back from a convenience store near her apartment. She remembers hearing a motorcycle idling nearby before it came closer, and then men's voices, one of them suddenly raised in Arabic. The sharp smell of alcohol hit her before she fully understood what was happening. What stayed with her most was the combination of those sensations-the engine noise, the shouting, the stale liquor on someone's breath-so that the event now lives in her as much through sound and smell as through images.

In the weeks afterward, those cues began to pull the memory back with shocking speed. A motorcycle passing her street could bring back the whole scene without warning, and if she heard men shouting in Arabic from a passing car or from a phone video somewhere in public, she would freeze and feel the assault rush back in full force. When the memory came, she did not just think about what happened; she heard the voices in her head as if they were happening again and sometimes caught the smell of alcohol so vividly that she would look around to see where it was coming from. Over time, the memories themselves seemed to make the world more densely packed with danger cues. After one of these episodes, even ordinary sounds and smells seemed to acquire the shape of the assault, so that a revving engine half a block away or liquor on a stranger in line could feel newly charged, as if the memory itself had taught her what else to fear. She had become so sensitized to engine noise, raised male voices, and the smell of liquor that she noticed them everywhere, and ordinary surroundings began to feel littered with traps.

Emily came to believe that what happened had destroyed her basic assumptions about how the world worked. Before the assault, she said, she had assumed that if she was careful and did the right things, she would be safe; now she was certain that safety could vanish instantly and for no reason. She also judged herself harshly. She was convinced that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, that another woman would have fought back, run faster, or somehow known what to do. Hearing a motorcycle rev or catching alcohol on a stranger's breath did not just trigger fear; it also brought a flood of self-condemning thoughts about being weak and no longer capable, as if those sensations proved again that she had been changed into someone less competent than she used to be.

Those beliefs fed directly into the way she now watches for danger. She listens at home for any sound that might mean someone is entering, especially at night, and she checks behind her repeatedly when she does go out, certain that if she misses one sign she will be caught off guard again. What frightened her most was not only the possibility of another assault but the conviction that she would fail again if something happened. When she had a flashback, that sense of present danger intensified; her body reacted as if the assault were happening again, and she would scan doors, windows, and hallways with desperate concentration. The more she monitored for threat, the more easily fragments of the assault broke through-voices, the engine, the smell-and each recurrence seemed to confirm for her that the world was unsafe and that she was no longer able to manage it. Living with that level of alarm day after day became, in her mind, its own proof: if she felt this unsafe all the time, she took it as evidence that the assault had permanently damaged her and that she was no longer the kind of person who could cope.

Her avoidance developed gradually but has become the structure of her days. She refuses to go out after dark, because nighttime feels inseparable from what happened and because every motorcycle or distant shout seems amplified once the sun goes down. She avoids dates connected to the assault, becoming tense and withdrawn as they approach, staying home and trying not to think about the calendar. She also avoids looking at or paying attention to her own body; even catching her reflection while dressing can stir up the memory too abruptly. At first these strategies felt like the only way to prevent being overwhelmed, but they have narrowed her life. Because she is unemployed, much of her time is spent inside the apartment, where she tries to control what she hears and smells, yet that has made her more reactive when she does encounter those cues. The strategies themselves had begun to mark the world with reminders: every evening she refused to step outside, every route she would not take, and every mirror she hurried past became another way the assault was kept present in daily life. The more thoroughly she organizes life around avoiding night, anniversaries, and her own body, the less chance she has to learn that a motorcycle passing by or alcohol on someone in a grocery line is not the assault happening again. Instead, each avoidance seems to preserve the rawness of the memory and strengthen her belief that she cannot cope. And because she leaves situations early, checks repeatedly, and structures her life around preventing the next jolt, she never remains anywhere long enough to discover that the danger her body predicts may not materialize, which keeps her sense of threat high.

Her husband has become used to finding her checking the locks repeatedly or pausing mid-conversation because she has heard a sound outside. She knows how young she is to feel this defeated, and that thought shames her further. By the time she sought help, she was spending most evenings braced for danger, scanning for noises, and dreading sudden sensory jolts that could pull her back into the assault. She came in because she feels her world shrinking and because she is terrified that this is permanent-that she will always live as if the next motorcycle, the next shouted phrase, or the next trace of alcohol means she is back there again.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state that intrusive trauma memories themselves lead to or increase triggers/reminders, rather than simply making her notice danger cues more often.
There is no paragraph explicitly conveying that her sense of threat causes or intensifies negative appraisals/beliefs, as opposed to beliefs feeding threat.
The vignette does not explicitly describe avoidance or other maladaptive strategies as causing or increasing triggers/reminders.
The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves increase her sense of threat, even though they preserve memory rawness and beliefs about not coping.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that intrusive trauma memories themselves lead to or increase triggers/reminders, rather than simply making her notice danger cues more often.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: There is no paragraph explicitly conveying that her sense of threat causes or intensifies negative appraisals/beliefs, as opposed to beliefs feeding threat.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly describe avoidance or other maladaptive strategies as causing or increasing triggers/reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies themselves increase her sense of threat, even though they preserve memory rawness and beliefs about not coping.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
